1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.name: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.background: First popularised by the Russian player Alexander Petrov in the mid-nineteenth century; in recognition of the early investigations by Petrov and Carl Jaenisch it is also called the Russian Game, the predominant name in some countries. World champions Smyslov, Petrosian, Karpov and Kramnik have all adopted it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn that Black left undefended. Black cannot simply retake on e4 at once, because the open e-file gives White tactics against the king, so the knight on e5 has to be driven off first. The game stays close to level: White has the first-move initiative, Black a very solid position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.background: Carl Jaenisch credited Alexander Petrov with the move, and Wilhelm Steinitz recommended it in his Modern Chess Instructor (1889), playing it three times against Pillsbury at St Petersburg 1895–96 for two wins and a draw. It came into vogue in the 1990s, when players such as Kasparov and Ivanchuk adopted it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Attacks the centre at once instead of grabbing a pawn, and lets Black choose which pawn to take. White opens the game early for fast development and activity, but the pawn exchanges that follow leave Black with a sound, roughly equal game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 with the queen, a solid-looking but awkward way: the queen blocks the f1 bishop, so the kingside cannot develop smoothly, and White has threatened nothing. Black can develop freely and fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: Petrov's Defence: Three Knights Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 by developing a piece and avoids the sharper lines of this defence. It is sound but modest: Black answers by developing the other knight and reaches a symmetrical, level position in which White has little to claim.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4.name: Petrov's Defence: Italian Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 at once but leaves e4 undefended. If Black takes the pawn, White hits the knight with a pawn and expects to win e5 back; if Black declines, the game is an ordinary balanced one. Sound, but it offers White little more than equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn that White left undefended and so makes White prove the gambit. The knight stands exposed on e4, but Black has several sound ways to defend it and either keep the extra pawn or return it on good terms.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nc6.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops the other knight, which defends e5. White's bishop already eyes f7, but Black has no weakness there, and the game takes a familiar, level course. A safe choice that gives up the chance of an extra pawn for a position without risk.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 d5.strategy: Hits the bishop at once and fights for the centre, accepting an open game while the king is still in the middle. Black has to be accurate there, and gives up the safety of simple development. Sharp, and sound enough.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3.name: Bishop's Opening: Boden-Kieseritzky Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3.background: Named after Samuel Boden and Lionel Kieseritzky; Boden published the first analysis of it in 1851.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3.strategy: Gambits the pawn for development: the knight attacks the one on e4, and after a trade White recaptures with the d-pawn, opening the c1-bishop and the d-file, with a knight jump to g5 against f7 in mind. Black can defend accurately, but White has real play for the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.d3.strategy: Hits the knight with a pawn instead of gambiting a pawn. Nothing defends the e5 pawn once the knight has to move, so White expects to win it back, and meanwhile opens the c1 bishop and builds a solid centre. It gives up the gambit's attacking chances for a level, low-risk game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the e5 pawn at once, but Black answers with a pawn that attacks the bishop, so White loses time retreating it. Material is level, but White is a tempo behind in development and Black's knight stays well placed in the centre. Playable, not ambitious.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3 d5.name: Bishop's Opening: Boden-Kieseritzky Gambit, Lichtenhein Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3 d5.strategy: Defends the knight with a pawn and attacks the bishop in the same move, taking a share of the centre instead of capturing on c3. White has to resolve the tension at once, and the game becomes open and tactical. A playable alternative to the main capture.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3 Nxc3.strategy: Takes the offered knight and accepts that White recaptures with the d-pawn to open the c1 bishop. Black then has to find the one pawn move that defends e5 and stops the knight jumping to g5; with it Black keeps the extra pawn at the cost of a slightly loosened king's side.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Declines the knight and develops, offering to trade on e4. If White takes, Black strikes at the bishop and knight with a pawn and the game is level, Black having given the extra pawn back for an easy position. A safe way to avoid the gambit's complications.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Retreats the knight and gives the pawn back: White takes on e5 and the position is roughly level. It avoids every gambit trick but achieves little, since Black has returned the extra pawn and White's bishop still eyes f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4.strategy: The main reply: Black takes the e4 pawn, and since White can retake on e5, the pawns are simply traded. The advanced knight needs support, but the symmetrical positions that follow are the soundest way to meet the early central strike, and give White at best a slight initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4.background: David Hooper recommended it in his 1967 book on 1.e4 e5. Today it is a minor sideline in modern tournament chess, where 3...Nxe4 is the clear preference.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn on d4 and keeps the extra pawn for now, but opens the e-file with the king still in the centre. White regains the pawn with tempo by attacking the knight, so Black spends time retreating. Sound and playable, but more passive than the main reply.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 d5.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Symmetrical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 d5.strategy: Meets the central strike with the d-pawn, which hands the decision about what to capture on e5 back to White. Solid and symmetrical, but it gives White the choice of structure: play usually transposes into the main lines, so Black gains nothing from the changed order.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5.strategy: Attacks the knight at once and gains space while the pawn on d4 is still hanging. Black has to spend time moving the knight, and White regains the pawn with the more active position, so Black's extra pawn does not last.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4.strategy: Gambits a pawn for quick development: the bishop eyes f7 and White can castle early. Black can keep the pawn and develop calmly, but White's lead in development roughly pays for it, so the game stays level and Black has to defend with care.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once but leaves e4 undefended: Black captures it, and after Qe2 pins the knight Black defends with ...Qe7 and keeps the extra pawn. The game is about level, but White is the one playing for equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4.strategy: Keeps the knight in the centre instead of retreating to the edge. It stands loose on e4, so White can regain the d4 pawn with an attack on it, and Black has to support it with a pawn at once; in return Black gets an open, active game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Qe7.strategy: Pins the e-pawn, so the attacked knight is safe for a moment, but White breaks the pin with a developing move and the knight has to run anyway. Black has only brought the queen out early, and White regains the d4 pawn with the better game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Nd5.strategy: Retreats to a square the queen hits at once: White recaptures on d4 with the queen, attacking the knight again. Black has lost the extra pawn and a tempo, and White has the lead in space and development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ng4.strategy: Runs to the edge, where a pawn move chases it again: h3 drives the knight away, White regains the d4 pawn and is clearly ahead in development. Black has taken a developed knight off its good square for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Centre Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Regains the pawn with the queen, which centralises and attacks the knight on e4 at the same time. Black has to defend or move the knight, and the queen on d4 is later exposed to Black's developing moves. The result is an open game in which White keeps a slight edge and both kings need care.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.background: Wilhelm Steinitz introduced the line in his 1889 book, where he recommended 5.Qe2 over the natural-looking 5.Qxd4.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Attacks the knight from a safe square and prepares to retake on d4 with the knight. It also sets a trap: defending with ...d5 fails to exd6 en passant, which pins the knight to the king along the e-file. Black has to move the knight again but can equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.B.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Tal Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.B.strategy: Pins the d-pawn, so that Black cannot support the e4 knight with ...d5, and keeps the option of regaining the d4 pawn with an attack on the knight. The bishop goes to a square where ...c6 challenges it with tempo, and White's development stalls. Offbeat and double-edged.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Takes the knight out of the queen's attack to a square where it eyes e4 and d3, and accepts that White retakes the d4 pawn. Black keeps the piece active and the structure sound, but White has more space, and the knight on c5 gets in the way of the f8 bishop.

Gives check before the knight can be taken. The natural block 6.c3 fails to 6...dxc3, since after 7.Qxe4 the pawn captures on b2 with a discovered check from the bishop, so White has to trade pieces instead and Black reaches an equal game.
Defends the knight with the pawn, but White takes it en passant with 6.exd6, and the knight on e4 is then pinned to the king by the queen and cannot recapture. Black loses a piece.

Regains the pawn with the knight, which lands on a strong central square and eyes c6 and e6, while the queen on e2 guards the pawn on e5. Material is level and White has the space, but the knight on d4 is not defended, which Black can use at once.

Develops with a gain of time by attacking the queen, and keeps the d4 pawn under fire. It is sound, but it does not regain the pawn by force, and Black can trade the dark-squared bishops to ease the cramped position.

Develops the knight to a square the d4 pawn cannot hit, but it blocks the c1 bishop and lets Black defend the pawn, so White still has to work to regain it. Sound, but slower than taking the pawn at once.
Hangs the knight: the pawn on d4 attacks c3, so ...dxc3 wins a piece for a pawn and White has no compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Bardeleben Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Develops with a double attack: the knight hits the undefended knight on d4 and the pawn on e5, so White has to resolve the tension at once. Black has regained the material and develops freely, and the pawn on e5, guarded only by the queen, stays a target.

Offers the exchange of knights at once, to get rid of the strong knight on d4. Black then recaptures with a pawn, which solves the problem of the knight but leaves White's pawn on e5 cramping Black's pieces. Playable but passive.

Develops the king's bishop and prepares to castle, but leaves White's knight on d4 alone. White simply develops and keeps the strong central knight and the space the pawn on e5 gives, so Black stays cramped without counterplay and ends clearly worse.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Centre Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop with a direct attack on the e4 knight, so Black has to defend it or prepare a tactical answer, and keeps White free to retake on e5 later. White is a pawn down only for the moment and gets the more active development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.dxe5.strategy: Retakes with the d-pawn, which clears the d-file so that the queen can come to d5, hitting the knight on e4 and f7. White avoids the symmetrical structure of the main line and plays for a sharper, unbalanced game, at the cost of giving up the central d-pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Nxe5.strategy: Regains the pawn with the knight at once. It is playable, but it lets Black choose the structure: Black can attack the knight with a pawn and head for the classical main line, so White gains nothing by capturing early.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5.strategy: Supports the knight with a pawn, takes a share of the centre and opens the c8 bishop. The structure is symmetrical once White retakes on e5, and the knight is well placed on e4; the cost is that the d-pawn can no longer chase White's knight from e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 Nc6.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Murrey Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 Nc6.strategy: Leaves the knight on e4 undefended as bait: if White takes it with the bishop, ...d5 leaves the bishop no good retreat and ...e4 forks bishop and knight, winning the piece back. If White declines, Black has developed quickly but gives White the choice of structure, and White keeps a slight edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 Nf6.strategy: Retreats the knight to where it started. White retakes on e5 with the d-pawn, which attacks the knight again, so Black has lost time while White has a developed bishop and a space edge. The extra pawn has gone back without any gain.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 exd4.strategy: Grabs a second pawn but leaves the knight on e4 undefended: Bxe4 wins it, and the trick of ...d5 and ...e4 no longer works because the e-pawn has left the e-file. White has a piece for two pawns, with the pawn on d4 still to collect.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.N.strategy: Retakes the pawn, restoring material equality and centralising the knight, which the d-pawn defends. Black can no longer drive it away with ...d6, since the pawn already stands on d5, so Black has to challenge it by other means. The position is symmetrical and level, with White's knight the more active piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.d.strategy: Retakes the pawn with the d-pawn instead of the knight. White gets a pawn on e5 and an asymmetrical structure rather than the symmetrical main line, and the d-file opens. Black's knight stays well supported by the d-pawn, so the game is level, with White playing for more imbalance.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.N.strategy: Attacks the knight a second time with a developing move, but leaves the e5 pawn alone, so White does not win the pawn back: after ...Nxd2 and the recapture, ...e4 hits the bishop, and Black keeps the extra pawn and the space.

Challenges the knight on e5 at once and develops the bishop for castling, keeping the position fully symmetrical. A solid choice that was once a main reply and is now played less often than the alternatives.

Attacks the centralised knight with the queenside knight, so White has to trade or retreat, while Black's bishops stay free to choose their squares. The usual trade develops the c8 bishop for free, at the price of a more tactical game around the knight on e4.

Attacks the centralised knight with the other knight. After White takes on c6, Black has to recapture with the b-pawn, which doubles the c-pawns and damages the structure. Playable, but it concedes something for no clear gain.

Castles to secure the king before the position opens. The knight on e5 is defended by the d-pawn, so the bishop's attack costs White nothing, and White prepares to challenge Black's centre. The game stays symmetrical and balanced.

Strikes at the d5 pawn that supports the knight on e4, the usual plan against this set-up, but plays it before castling. Black can answer with a check from b4 or trade on e5, so White gains nothing by force and the game stays level.

Challenges the knight on e4 with a developing move, though it blocks the c1 bishop for now. If Black trades on d2 and then on e5, White ends with the two bishops and a pawn on e5, a small space edge; Black's position stays solid and level.

Mirrors White: the king is safe and the structure stays fully symmetrical. Neither side has a clear way to profit at once, and the game turns on which of them can better challenge the other's advanced knight, Black's on e4 or White's on e5.

Trades the bishop for White's centralised knight at once. White recaptures with the d-pawn and gets a pawn on e5 and more space, while Black keeps the knight on e4 firmly supported. The game stays level, but Black gives up the dark-squared bishop that would otherwise fight against that pawn.
Adds a second defender to the knight on e4, but loses material: after f3 the knight is attacked by a pawn and cannot move without leaving the bishop on f5 to the bishop on d3.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the other knight, the most common and best-regarded reply. Both sides now have both knights out, and the game takes a symmetrical, classical course that avoids the lines special to this defence. Black is solid and level, with White having little to claim.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the knight on c3 to the king and invites White to take the pawn on e5. Black castles, attacks e4 and gets the pawn back after exchanging the bishop for the knight, which gives White the two bishops. Active, and it leaves White only a slight edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and keeps the set-up compact, with the c8 bishop free to develop. It is solid but passive: White can occupy the centre at once and Black has less space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6.strategy: A natural developing reply: the knight guards e5 and joins the fight for d4, while White's queen, standing in front of its own bishop, has nothing to attack. Black gets easy development and can aim for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn instead of a piece, giving Black a compact and solid structure with little to attack. The price is space: the pawn on d6 shuts in the c8-bishop for now, so Black accepts a cramped but safe game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 with the queen, so taking on e5 would only lose a knight for a pawn. It is safe but awkward: the queen blocks the f8-bishop, and Black's development is slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.d4.name: Petrov's Defence: Moody Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once and offers a pawn: after ...exd4 the knight cannot retake because ...Nxd4 wins it, but e5 hits the knight on f6 and White regains the pawn. The queen still shuts in the f1-bishop, yet the game stays level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares to take the centre with a pawn supported from c3, while the queen already guards e4. It is the plan that suits the early queen move: White builds a broad pawn centre and answers Black's pressure on e4 calmly.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.d3.strategy: Guards e4 with a pawn and frees the c1-bishop, a solid set-up in which everything is protected. It is passive, though: the f1-bishop is still shut in behind the queen and Black can claim the centre at once.
